cards.subject: A user story
says: describes a need from the viewpoint of the person who wants it
is commonly phrased as who, what and why
is kept small enough to finish within one iteration
cards.use: want to capture a need without prescribing the solution
not: is a detailed technical specification of how to build the feature

cards.subject: A use case
says: describes the steps of an interaction between an actor and a system
lists a main success path and alternative flows
names the actor who starts the interaction
cards.use: need to spell out the error and alternative paths of an interaction
not: is always a single sentence

cards.subject: A problem statement
says: says who has the problem, what happens today and what outcome is wanted
is kept separate from any proposed solution
is agreed before a solution is priced
cards.use: hear a client describe a solution before describing the need
not: names the technology the team will use

cards.subject: MoSCoW prioritisation
says: sorts requirements into must, should, could and won't have
makes the won't-have-this-time list explicit
keeps must-haves to the minimum a release cannot do without
cards.use: need to agree what to cut first when time runs short
not: ranks every requirement with a unique number from one to n

cards.subject: A non-functional requirement
says: describes how well the system must behave rather than what it does
covers qualities such as performance, security and availability
is often missed because nobody asks for it
cards.use: need to state how fast or how available the system must be
not: is optional once the functional requirements are met

cards.subject: An out-of-scope list
says: names what the project will not deliver
protects both sides by making a clear no visible
is agreed alongside what is in scope
cards.use: want to prevent assumptions about work that was never promised
not: is only needed once the project is late

cards.subject: A requirements traceability matrix
says: links each requirement to its design, test and delivery items
shows which requirements have no test
helps assess which items a change would touch
cards.use: must prove that every requirement was built and tested
not: lists only the tasks assigned to each person

cards.subject: The Kano model
says: separates basic expectations, performance needs and delighters
shows that today's delighter tends to become tomorrow's expectation
cards.use: want to decide which features create delight and which only avoid complaints
not: scores features strictly by development cost

cards.subject: Moksy's discovery
says: aims to understand the problem before a solution is priced
starts by confirming the problem statement
comes before an estimate rather than after it
cards.use: want to know why Moksy confirms the problem before quoting
not: prices the solution first and refines the problem afterwards

cards.subject: An estimate
says: is a forecast rather than a promise
is most useful when it says how sure you are
should follow the requirements rather than a one-line idea
cards.use: are asked for a number on work that is still vague
not: is a commitment that must never be revised

cards.subject: A three-point estimate
says: gives a best case, a most likely case and a worst case
can be combined into a weighted expected value
shows the spread of uncertainty instead of one number
cards.use: want to express uncertainty for a single task
not: averages the guesses of three different teams

cards.subject: A bottom-up estimate
says: sums the estimates of small work packages
needs the work broken down first
benefits from individual errors tending to average out
cards.use: have a detailed breakdown and want a total you can defend
not: starts from a fixed budget and divides it among the parts

cards.subject: An analogous estimate
says: starts from the actual size of a similar past project
is quick but only as good as the similarity
suits early stages when little detail exists
cards.use: need a rough figure fast from a comparable earlier job
not: is built from a full task breakdown

cards.subject: Planning poker
says: has each person reveal an estimate card at the same time
exposes disagreement so it can be discussed
reduces anchoring on the first number spoken
cards.use: want the whole team to size backlog items without anyone dominating
not: lets the product owner set the final number

cards.subject: Story points
says: measure relative size rather than hours
combine effort, complexity and uncertainty
are meaningful mainly within one team
cards.use: want to size backlog items without committing to hours
not: convert to a fixed number of hours that applies to every team

cards.subject: Contingency
says: is an explicit allowance for uncertainty
is shown openly rather than padded into every line
grows when requirements are vague
cards.use: want to cover unknowns without hiding padding
not: is a secret buffer the client is not told about

cards.subject: The cone of uncertainty
says: shows estimate error narrowing as the project progresses
explains why early estimates need wide ranges
is widest at the very start of a project
cards.use: must explain why a day-one estimate cannot be tight
not: says early estimates are the most accurate

cards.subject: Effort
says: is the amount of work measured in person-hours or person-days
excludes the time the work spends waiting
adds up across people working in parallel
cards.use: need to say how much work is involved, not how long it takes
not: is the elapsed calendar time between start and finish

cards.subject: Duration
says: is the elapsed calendar time from start to finish
stretches when work waits for client feedback
can be much longer than the effort it contains
cards.use: need to tell the client when the work will be done
not: is the sum of person-hours on a task

cards.subject: Commonly forgotten work items
says: include testing, review rounds, deployment and handover
include client content and project management
explain why an estimate built only from coding is too low
cards.use: check an estimate for pieces nobody listed
not: are covered automatically by the build estimate

cards.subject: The planning fallacy
says: is the tendency to underestimate time even when similar tasks overran before
is countered by comparing earlier estimates with actuals
cards.use: see a plan that ignores how long similar work took last time
not: affects only inexperienced people

cards.subject: Reference class forecasting
says: bases a forecast on the outcomes of many similar past projects
corrects optimism by taking an outside view
adjusts the baseline figure using the spread of past results
cards.use: must counter a sponsor's optimistic view of a single project
not: relies only on the team's detailed plan for this project

cards.subject: A project charter
says: authorises the project
names the objectives, the sponsor and the project manager
gives the manager authority to use resources
cards.use: need formal permission and a mandate to begin
not: is the detailed task-by-task schedule

cards.subject: A work breakdown structure
says: decomposes the deliverables into smaller work packages
is organised by deliverable rather than by date
covers the whole scope, with children adding up to the parent
cards.use: need to be sure no part of the scope is missed when planning
not: is a calendar of when each person works

cards.subject: A Gantt chart
says: shows tasks as bars along a timeline
can display dependencies between tasks
makes overlapping work visible at a glance
cards.use: want to show tasks against calendar dates
not: breaks the deliverables into a hierarchy without dates

cards.subject: A milestone
says: marks a significant point in the plan
has zero duration
is a checkpoint for review and decisions
cards.use: want a visible checkpoint to review progress
not: is a task that takes several weeks

cards.subject: A baseline
says: is the approved scope, schedule and cost that progress is measured against
changes only through change control
lets variance be calculated
cards.use: need a fixed reference to measure drift
not: is updated silently whenever the plan slips

cards.subject: The critical path
says: is the longest chain of dependent tasks
sets the shortest possible project duration
has no float
cards.use: need to know which delays will move the end date
not: is the list of the most expensive tasks

cards.subject: Float
says: is how long a task can slip without moving the project end date
is also called slack in scheduling
is the difference between a task's earliest and latest start
cards.use: want to know which tasks can absorb a delay
not: is extra budget held for risks

cards.subject: Finish-to-start
says: means the successor cannot start until the predecessor finishes
is the most common dependency type
fits testing that must follow a finished build
cards.use: need one task to wait until another is done
not: lets two tasks run completely in parallel

cards.subject: A hard dependency
says: is inherent in the nature of the work
cannot be reordered, such as testing a feature before it exists
is also called mandatory
cards.use: see an order that logic forces on the tasks
not: is a preference the team can change freely

cards.subject: A soft dependency
says: is an order chosen by preference or good practice
can be changed to compress the schedule
is also called discretionary
cards.use: want to know which sequence can be reordered when time is short
not: is forced by the nature of the work

cards.subject: Rolling-wave planning
says: plans near-term work in detail and later work at a high level
refines later phases as understanding grows
cards.use: face a long project where the later work is still unclear
not: fixes every task of the whole project in detail on day one

cards.subject: A sprint
says: is a fixed-length iteration
produces a usable increment by its end
is followed immediately by the next one
cards.use: want a regular rhythm of delivery and feedback
not: ends only when all planned work is finished, however long that takes

cards.subject: Sprint planning
says: selects the work for the coming sprint
agrees a sprint goal
lets the team decide how much it can take on
cards.use: start a sprint and must decide what fits
not: is where the product owner assigns tasks to individuals

cards.subject: The daily stand-up
says: is a short daily sync of the team
focuses on coordinating work toward the sprint goal
is not a status report to a manager
cards.use: want the team to spot blockers each day
not: is held weekly for stakeholders

cards.subject: The sprint review
says: demonstrates the increment to stakeholders
collects feedback that shapes the backlog
looks at the product rather than the team's process
cards.use: want stakeholder feedback on working software
not: inspects how the team works together

cards.subject: The product backlog
says: is an ordered list of what might be needed in the product
is never complete and changes as understanding grows
has its ordering owned by one person
cards.use: need a single place for all upcoming work
not: is frozen at the start of the project

cards.subject: Backlog refinement
says: clarifies, splits and orders upcoming items
prepares items so they are ready for planning
is ongoing rather than a single event
cards.use: find upcoming stories too big or vague to start
not: happens only after the sprint ends

cards.subject: The product owner
says: orders the backlog by value
decides what is built next
speaks for the stakeholders
cards.use: need someone accountable for what the team builds
not: assigns individual tasks to developers

cards.subject: The scrum master
says: coaches the team on the process
removes impediments
does not assign tasks or manage the people
cards.use: need someone to help the team follow its agreed way of working
not: decides the order of the backlog

cards.subject: A spike
says: is a time-boxed investigation to reduce uncertainty
produces knowledge rather than a shippable feature
ends with a decision or a better estimate
cards.use: must find out whether an approach is feasible before committing
not: is a feature delivered to users at the end of the sprint

cards.subject: A minimum viable product
says: is the smallest release that tests a key assumption with real users
exists to learn whether the idea works
cards.use: want to learn whether the idea works before building the full thing
not: includes every feature planned for the first year

cards.subject: Velocity
says: is the amount of work a team completes per sprint
is used to forecast how much will fit in future sprints
should not be compared between teams
cards.use: need a basis to forecast how many sprints the backlog needs
not: measures each individual's productivity

cards.subject: A burndown chart
says: plots remaining work against time
slopes down toward zero as work is finished
does not show added scope separately
cards.use: want to see whether the sprint is on track to finish
not: shows the cumulative amount of work completed against a total scope line

cards.subject: A burnup chart
says: shows completed work rising toward a total scope line
makes changes in scope visible as the scope line moving
cards.use: must show the client that the target moved, not that the team slowed
not: hides scope growth because the total is fixed

cards.subject: Cycle time
says: is measured from when work starts on an item to when it is done
is the part of lead time that the team directly controls
cards.use: want to know how long the team takes once it begins an item
not: starts when the customer first makes the request

cards.subject: Lead time
says: is measured from the request arriving to delivery
includes the time spent waiting in the queue
is what the customer experiences
cards.use: want to know how long a customer waits from asking to receiving
not: starts only when a developer picks the item up

cards.subject: Throughput
says: counts the items finished per unit of time
can feed a forecast of how many items will be done by a date
cards.use: need to know how many items the team finishes each week
not: measures how long each item took

cards.subject: Work in progress
says: counts items started but not yet finished
rises when people begin new work before finishing old work
pushes cycle time up as it grows
cards.use: see many items open and few completed
not: counts the items completed per week

cards.subject: A cumulative flow diagram
says: stacks the number of items in each state over time
shows a widening band where work is piling up
can show lead time and work in progress as distances on the chart
cards.use: want to spot a bottleneck forming across states
not: plots remaining story points against days left in a sprint

cards.subject: Little's Law
says: relates average work in progress, throughput and cycle time
says average cycle time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput
explains why cutting work in progress shortens cycle time
cards.use: must show why limiting work in progress makes delivery faster
not: predicts exactly how many defects a release will have

cards.subject: Monte Carlo forecasting
says: runs many simulations sampled from historical throughput
gives the probability of finishing by a date rather than a single date
needs reasonably stable historical data
cards.use: must give a date with a stated confidence rather than one number
not: relies on a single expert's guess of the end date

cards.subject: A kanban board
says: visualises work as cards in columns by state
shows where work is queued and blocked
cards.use: want everyone to see what is in progress
not: assigns every card to a fixed sprint

cards.subject: A WIP limit
says: caps the number of items allowed in a column or stage
forces the team to finish work before starting new work
exposes bottlenecks when a column fills
cards.use: see work piling up half-done
not: sets the maximum hours any one person may log per day

cards.subject: A pull system
says: starts new work only when capacity frees up
contrasts with pushing work in on a schedule
cards.use: want to avoid overloading a stage
not: assigns work to people the moment it arrives

cards.subject: A swimlane
says: separates types of work or teams in horizontal rows
lets urgent work be told apart from regular work at a glance
cards.use: need to show different kinds of work on one board
not: divides the board into vertical state columns

cards.subject: A class of service
says: gives different types of work different handling rules
may allow an expedite class with special rules
cards.use: must handle both urgent fixes and normal work on one board
not: gives every item the same priority

cards.subject: A bottleneck
says: is the stage whose capacity limits the throughput of the whole flow
shows as a queue building in front of it
is where improvement raises output the most
cards.use: see items waiting in front of one stage while later stages sit idle
not: is the stage with the most staff

cards.subject: Work item age
says: measures how long an item has been in progress so far
highlights items at risk of exceeding typical cycle time
cards.use: want to catch stuck items before they finish late
not: measures how long finished items took

cards.subject: A risk
says: is something that might happen and affect the project
has a probability and an impact
is managed before it happens
cards.use: spot a possible event that has not occurred yet
not: is a problem that has already occurred

cards.subject: An assumption
says: is something believed true but not yet confirmed
becomes a risk or an issue if it proves false
is written down so that its failure gives a basis for a change request
cards.use: plan around a fact the client has promised but not yet delivered
not: is a requirement that has been verified

cards.subject: An issue
says: is a problem that has already happened
needs action now rather than monitoring
cards.use: find that a blocker is already stopping work
not: has a probability of occurring

cards.subject: A dependency
says: is something the project needs from outside the team
can block progress when the other party is late
is recorded with the date by which the other party must deliver
cards.use: wait on a supplier's delivery or on client content
not: is a task the team fully controls

cards.subject: A decision
says: records what was decided, by whom and when
prevents the same question being reopened without reason
cards.use: need a traceable record of a choice
not: tracks a problem awaiting resolution

cards.subject: A constraint
says: is a fixed limit on the project such as a deadline or budget
limits the options the plan can use
cards.use: plan around a hard launch date set by an external event
not: is an uncertain event that might happen

cards.subject: An action
says: is a specific follow-up with an owner and a due date
comes out of a meeting or a review
cards.use: leave a meeting with a task that has no owner yet
not: records a choice that has already been made

cards.subject: A RAID log
says: tracks risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies in one place
is reviewed regularly rather than filled in once
cards.use: need one shared list of what could derail delivery
not: is a log of every code change made

cards.subject: A risk register
says: records each risk with probability, impact, owner and response
shows the status of each risk over time
cards.use: must track each risk to its owner and response
not: records only problems that have already happened

cards.subject: A probability and impact matrix
says: ranks risks by combining likelihood and consequence
plots probability on one axis and impact on the other
helps decide which risks need action first
cards.use: have a long risk list and must choose where to act first
not: records who is responsible for each risk

cards.subject: A risk trigger
says: is an early warning sign that a risk is about to occur
tells you when to start the contingency plan
cards.use: want a signal that a risk is becoming real
not: is the owner assigned to a risk

cards.subject: Risk avoidance
says: changes the plan so the risk cannot occur
removes the threat, for example by dropping a risky feature
cards.use: can remove the feature that creates the risk
not: moves the financial impact to a third party

cards.subject: Risk mitigation
says: reduces the probability or the impact of a risk
acts before the risk happens, for example by building an early prototype
cards.use: want to lower the likelihood of a risk without removing its cause
not: removes the risk entirely by changing the scope

cards.subject: Risk transfer
says: shifts the impact to a third party such as an insurer or a supplier
moves who bears the consequence without removing the risk
cards.use: want a supplier or insurer to carry the consequence
not: removes the cause of the risk

cards.subject: Risk acceptance
says: acknowledges the risk and takes no action unless it occurs
is chosen when the cost of a response exceeds the exposure
cards.use: decide that the cost of responding is greater than the exposure
not: lowers the probability before it occurs

cards.subject: A contingency plan
says: is carried out only if a trigger occurs
is prepared in advance of the risk happening
cards.use: want a ready response to run if a risk materialises
not: is the action taken to reduce likelihood before the risk occurs

cards.subject: A pre-mortem
says: imagines the project has already failed and asks why
surfaces risks people hesitate to raise
is run before work starts
cards.use: want to find risks before committing to a plan
not: analyses the causes of a failure that already happened

cards.subject: Scope creep
says: is uncontrolled growth in scope without a matching change in time or cost
often arrives as many small agreed yeses
cards.use: see small requests absorbed one by one
not: is a formally approved increase in scope

cards.subject: A change request
says: describes a proposed change to the agreed scope
carries an estimate of its effect on cost and date
cards.use: need a request to change what was agreed to be assessed
not: is raised only by the delivery team

cards.subject: A change log
says: is a visible record of every requested change and its decision
makes it possible to show how and why scope moved
cards.use: must show how scope moved over the project
not: lists the code changes in each release

cards.subject: An impact assessment
says: estimates the effect of a change on cost, time, quality and risk
is done before approval, not after
cards.use: are asked to approve a change without knowing its cost
not: is written after the change has been delivered

cards.subject: A change control board
says: reviews proposed changes and approves or rejects them
includes people who can commit budget and priorities
cards.use: need a body that can approve changes above a threshold
not: writes the code for approved changes

cards.subject: Gold plating
says: adds features nobody asked for
is done by the delivery team on its own initiative
cards.use: find the team polishing extras the client never requested
not: is growth in scope requested by the client

cards.subject: Written client approval
says: makes decisions traceable
confirms in writing what was agreed
cards.use: need evidence of what the client agreed
not: is unnecessary when the conversation was friendly

cards.subject: A fixed-price contract
says: fixes the price for an agreed scope
puts the cost of overruns mainly on the supplier
makes change control essential
cards.use: want the price known up front for a well-defined scope
not: bills for the actual effort spent

cards.subject: A time-and-materials contract
says: bills for the actual effort spent
puts the cost of overruns mainly on the client
suits work whose scope cannot be fixed up front
cards.use: face scope that cannot be defined before work begins
not: fixes the price for an agreed scope

cards.subject: The iron triangle
says: links scope, time and cost so a change to one affects the others
is also called the triple constraint
cards.use: must explain why a bigger scope cannot keep the same date and cost
not: says scope, time and cost can each be changed independently

cards.subject: RAG status
says: uses red, amber and green to summarise health
treats amber as at risk but recoverable
cards.use: want a quick traffic-light summary of project health
not: shows the percentage of tasks completed

cards.subject: A status report
says: tells stakeholders where the project stands, what is next and what needs a decision
is short and regular
cards.use: must update stakeholders on a regular rhythm
not: is written only when the project ends

cards.subject: Watermelon reporting
says: shows green on the outside while the detail underneath is red
hides trouble until it is too late to fix cheaply
cards.use: see a project reported green for weeks and then missing a date
not: reports every minor variance to the board

cards.subject: Exception reporting
says: reports only deviations beyond an agreed tolerance
reduces noise for senior readers
cards.use: want senior readers to hear only when something is outside tolerance
not: reports every task every week

cards.subject: An escalation path
says: defines who to go to when an issue cannot be solved at the current level
names the next person before the problem arises
cards.use: cannot resolve a blocker at team level
not: is a list of everyone who receives the status report

cards.subject: A steering committee
says: provides senior governance
unblocks decisions the project manager cannot make
reviews progress against objectives at intervals
cards.use: need senior sponsors to unblock a decision
not: does the day-to-day tasks of the project

cards.subject: An early warning
says: raises a slip as soon as it is known
leaves time to respond before the date is missed
cards.use: learn of a slip and must decide when to tell the sponsor
not: waits for the next milestone before mentioning a slip

cards.subject: The schedule performance index
says: is earned value divided by planned value
below 1 means the project is behind schedule
cards.use: want to know whether progress matches the plan
not: is earned value divided by actual cost

cards.subject: The cost performance index
says: is earned value divided by actual cost
below 1 means the project is over budget
cards.use: want to know whether money is being spent efficiently for the work done
not: is earned value divided by planned value

cards.subject: The definition of done
says: is a shared checklist every item must meet to count as complete
applies to all items rather than to a single story
includes the team's common quality bar such as reviewed and tested
cards.use: need one common standard for finished work
not: is written separately for each story by the client

cards.subject: An acceptance criterion
says: is a testable condition a single story must satisfy to be accepted
is specific to one item
is agreed before the work starts
cards.use: need to agree how one story will be judged complete
not: applies unchanged to every item the team delivers

cards.subject: User acceptance testing
says: is done by the client or end users
confirms the solution meets their real needs
happens before final acceptance
cards.use: need the client to confirm the solution works for them
not: is done only by the developers who built it

cards.subject: Given-When-Then
says: writes a criterion as a context, an action and an expected outcome
can be turned directly into automated tests
cards.use: want acceptance criteria that read as scenarios
not: lists tasks and their owners

cards.subject: A quality gate
says: blocks progress until the agreed checks pass
is applied at a defined point such as before a release
cards.use: want a release blocked until the checks pass
not: is advisory and can be skipped under pressure

cards.subject: Technical debt
says: is the future cost of shortcuts taken now
accrues interest as it is ignored
cards.use: see quick fixes piling up that will slow later work
not: is money owed to a supplier

cards.subject: Defect severity
says: describes the impact of a defect on the system or user
is set by assessing the harm caused
cards.use: must rate how much damage a defect does
not: describes how soon a defect should be fixed

cards.subject: Defect priority
says: describes how soon a defect should be fixed
can differ from severity, such as a harmless typo on the home page
cards.use: must decide the order in which defects are fixed
not: describes the harm a defect does to the system

cards.subject: A retrospective
says: is a regular meeting where the team inspects its own way of working
ends with a small number of agreed improvements
looks at the process rather than the product
cards.use: want the team to improve how it works
not: demonstrates the finished increment to stakeholders

cards.subject: Start-stop-continue
says: sorts feedback into things to start, stop and keep doing
cards.use: want a simple format for a first retrospective
not: rates each team member's performance

cards.subject: The five whys
says: asks why repeatedly to move from symptom to root cause
stops at a cause the team can act on
cards.use: need the root cause behind a recurring problem
not: lists the five most senior stakeholders

cards.subject: A blameless post-mortem
says: examines an incident's causes in systems and process rather than in individuals
produces follow-up actions with owners
cards.use: must learn from an outage without punishing people
not: names the person at fault in the report

cards.subject: A lessons-learned register
says: records what to repeat or avoid on later projects
is reviewed at the start of new projects
cards.use: want the next project to benefit from this one
not: is filled in once and archived unread

cards.subject: Psychological safety
says: is the belief that you can speak up without being punished
is a precondition for honest retrospectives
cards.use: see a team that stays silent in retrospectives
not: means nobody ever disagrees

cards.subject: A retrospective action
says: has an owner and a date
is reviewed at the next retrospective
is kept to a few so that they get done
cards.use: find that the same problem is raised in retrospective after retrospective
not: is a list of every complaint raised

cards.subject: Capacity
says: is the amount of work a person or team can take on in a period
is reduced by leave, meetings and support work
cards.use: must plan how much work fits in a sprint or month
not: is the total number of people on the payroll

cards.subject: Utilisation
says: is the share of available time spent on planned work
is a measure of how busy people are rather than of what they achieve
cards.use: want to know how busy a team is
not: is the amount of work completed per sprint

cards.subject: Resource levelling
says: adjusts the schedule to resolve overallocated people
may push out the end date
cards.use: find a person booked at more than their capacity
not: adds people to the project to finish earlier

cards.subject: The bus factor
says: counts how many people could be lost before the project stalls
is low when one person alone holds critical knowledge
cards.use: worry that one person alone knows how to deploy
not: measures how many vehicles a team uses

cards.subject: Brooks's law
says: says adding people to a late software project makes it later
arises from training and communication overhead
cards.use: are asked to add developers to a late project
not: says more people always shorten delivery

cards.subject: Context switching
says: wastes capacity when one person splits attention across several tasks
grows with the number of concurrent items
cards.use: see people spread thinly across many tasks
not: improves throughput by keeping everyone busy

cards.subject: A RACI matrix
says: assigns each task a Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed party
has exactly one Accountable party per task
cards.use: need clarity on who decides and who does
not: lists the risks by probability and impact

cards.subject: Slack capacity
says: leaves headroom for unplanned work
keeps queues from growing sharply as load rises
cards.use: must absorb urgent requests without derailing planned work
not: is wasted time that should be scheduled away

cards.subject: A handover
says: is the planned transfer of knowledge, access and responsibility
is complete when the client can operate the system
applies to people leaving as well as to projects
cards.use: finish building and must leave the client able to run it
not: is finished when the code is deployed

cards.subject: A handover package
says: lists where things live, such as hosting, domains and repositories
explains how to deploy and roll back
records how backups work, who to contact and the known issues
cards.use: prepare what the client needs to run the system without you
not: contains only the source code

cards.subject: A runbook
says: is a short guide to common jobs and failures
gives step-by-step instructions for the person on duty
cards.use: want the client to handle routine jobs and failures alone
not: describes the full product vision

cards.subject: Account ownership transfer
says: moves accounts to the client rather than the supplier's personal login
avoids the client depending on an individual's account
cards.use: find the client's domain registered under a developer's personal login
not: leaves accounts under the supplier so support is easier

cards.subject: Secure credential transfer
says: sends credentials through a secure channel
keeps secrets out of plain email and chat
cards.use: must give the client access to hosting
not: pastes passwords into the project chat

cards.subject: A walkthrough session
says: shows the people who will use or maintain the system how it works
is held with the real users, not only the sponsor
cards.use: want the people who will run the system to see it working
not: replaces the written handover notes entirely

cards.subject: A support statement
says: states what ongoing support covers
states the response times that apply
cards.use: need the client to know what to expect after handover
not: promises unlimited changes at no charge

cards.subject: Acceptance sign-off
says: is the client's formal confirmation that deliverables meet the agreed criteria
marks the point at which the deliverables are accepted
cards.use: need written proof that the client accepted the work
not: is given automatically when the code is deployed

cards.subject: A rollback plan
says: defines how to return to the previous state if a release fails
is tested before it is needed
cards.use: must be able to undo a release within minutes
not: describes how to add new features after launch

cards.subject: A post-implementation review
says: checks some time after go-live whether the intended benefits were realised
feeds lessons into future projects
cards.use: want to know whether the project delivered what was promised
not: happens on the day of go-live

cards.subject: gglearn's handovers table
says: holds handover notes per person
can tie a note to a learning track
cards.use: want to know where gglearn keeps handover notes
not: stores customer invoices

cards.subject: gglearn's offboarding checklist
says: starts with writing handover notes for each area you own
includes transferring ownership of accounts, files and customers
includes recording the answers to the ten questions only you know
includes returning equipment and revoking tool access
cards.use: want to know what a leaver does in gglearn
not: leaves tool access in place so the leaver can help later

cards.subject: Client continuity
says: keeps a record above the single project
avoids restarting each project from zero
remembers who the client is, what they do and what was decided
cards.use: find a returning client being asked the same questions again
not: ends when the first project is delivered

cards.subject: A holder
says: is the person or organisation above the project
carries a profile of what is known about them
cards.use: want to know what the continuity brief calls the person or business above a project
not: is a confirmed problem lifted off a project

cards.subject: A profile
says: holds what is known about the holder
records each fact with an origin and an age
cards.use: want to tell which facts about a client are stale
not: is the person or organisation above the project

cards.subject: A challenge
says: is a confirmed problem lifted off the project
is versioned
has the projects tackling it joined to it
cards.use: get a second project on the same problem
not: is a person or organisation above the project

cards.subject: The origin of a fact
says: records where a fact came from and when
shows which facts have become stale
cards.use: must decide whether to trust an old fact about a client
not: is the date the client signed the contract

cards.subject: A read-back
says: plays the problem back to the client field by field
happens before anything is priced
cards.use: want to confirm the problem was understood before quoting
not: sends the client the final invoice

cards.subject: The nine problem fields
says: exist on the project in the continuity brief
carry the origin of each statement, the quote and a confidence
cards.use: want to see where each statement about a problem came from
not: list the nine phases of a delivery project

cards.subject: The customer-continuity brief
says: is at founder review
describes a design rather than built behaviour
lists stages including attach, recall and confirm
cards.use: are asked whether Moksy's continuity design is live
not: is already running in production for every customer

cards.subject: A client's ask
says: is not the same as the problem behind it
can hide a different problem, such as a website request hiding a lead-generation problem
cards.use: hear a client ask for a website
not: is always the real problem to price

qa.q: What does RAID stand for in a project log?
qa.right: Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies
qa.why: A RAID log tracks the four things that can derail delivery.

qa.q: Which statement best describes an estimate?
qa.right: A forecast that is most useful when it says how sure you are
wrong: A promise of the exact date and cost
A number agreed once and never revisited
The client's budget restated as hours
qa.why: An estimate is a forecast with stated uncertainty, not a commitment.

qa.q: Who owns the ordering of the product backlog?
qa.right: The product owner
qa.why: The product owner orders the backlog by value.

qa.q: What is the main effect of a WIP limit on a kanban board?
qa.right: It forces the team to finish work before starting new work
wrong: It caps the hours each person may work
It stops new requests from being accepted at all
It sets the number of sprints in a release
qa.why: Limiting work in progress shortens queues and exposes bottlenecks.

qa.q: What is scope creep?
qa.right: Uncontrolled growth in scope without a matching change in time or cost
wrong: A formally approved addition to scope
The team delivering less than agreed
A delay caused by late client feedback
qa.why: Scope creep happens when changes are absorbed without being assessed.

qa.q: In a RAG status report, what does amber normally mean?
qa.right: At risk but recoverable with action
qa.why: Amber warns that the project is drifting but can still be recovered.

qa.q: Which meeting is for the team to inspect its own way of working?
qa.right: The retrospective
qa.why: The sprint review inspects the product; the retrospective inspects the process.

qa.q: A task needs 20 hours of work, but the only reviewer is available for two hours each Friday. Which statement is true?
qa.right: Effort is 20 hours, but duration is much longer because of waiting
wrong: Duration is 20 hours because duration equals effort
Effort is longer than duration because of waiting
Both are one week because the work is done on Fridays
qa.why: Effort is work content; duration is elapsed calendar time, which includes waiting.

qa.q: What is this format used for?
qa.right: Writing an acceptance criterion as a context, an action and an expected outcome
wrong: Recording a risk with its probability and impact
qa.why: Given-When-Then expresses criteria as testable scenarios.
qa.code:
Given a customer with an empty basket
When they add one item
Then the basket count shows 1

qa.q: A team's average work in progress is 12 items and its average throughput is 3 items per week. By Little's Law, what is the average cycle time?
qa.right: 4 weeks
qa.why: Cycle time equals work in progress divided by throughput: 12 / 3 = 4.

qa.q: Earned value is 80, planned value is 100 and actual cost is 90. What are the schedule and cost performance indices?
qa.right: SPI 0.8 (behind schedule) and CPI about 0.89 (over budget)
wrong: SPI 1.25 and CPI 1.12, ahead of schedule and under budget
qa.why: SPI is earned value over planned value; CPI is earned value over actual cost.
qa.code:
EV = 80
PV = 100
AC = 90
SPI = EV / PV
CPI = EV / AC

qa.q: Tasks: A (3 days) then C (4 days); B (5 days) then C; C then D (2 days). What is the project duration and the critical path?
qa.right: 11 days, along B, C, D
wrong: 14 days, because all tasks are summed
qa.why: The longest chain, B 5 + C 4 + D 2, sets the duration. A has 2 days of float.

qa.q: In the previous schedule, how much float does task A have?
qa.right: 2 days
qa.why: A (3 days) can slip until it equals B (5 days) before delaying C, so it has 2 days of float.

qa.q: A client asks in week 6 for 'just one more button'. What should you do first?
qa.right: Describe the change, estimate its effect on cost and date, and get approval before doing it
wrong: Add it quietly to keep the client happy
Add it and mention the cost in the final invoice
qa.why: Every change goes through assessment and approval, even small ones.

qa.q: Which is a non-functional requirement?
qa.right: The checkout page must respond within two seconds under normal load
wrong: A user can add an item to the basket
An administrator can export orders as a spreadsheet
A customer receives a confirmation email
qa.why: Non-functional requirements describe how well the system behaves, not what it does.

qa.q: What does a story point measure?
qa.right: Relative size, combining effort, complexity and uncertainty
wrong: The business value of the story
qa.why: Points are relative to a team's own scale.

qa.q: Management wants to rank two teams by sprint velocity. What is the main problem?
qa.right: Story points are relative to each team, so velocities are not comparable
wrong: Velocity is only valid for teams of ten or more
Velocity is measured in hours, which differ by team
Velocity can only be measured once a quarter
qa.why: Velocity is for a team's own forecasting, not for comparing teams.

qa.q: The burndown chart stays flat although the team is clearly working. New items were added mid-sprint. Which chart would show this most clearly?
qa.right: A burnup chart
qa.why: A burnup chart shows completed work and the total scope line separately.

qa.q: A board has a WIP limit of 3 for Review and 9 cards in Review. What should the team do?
qa.right: Stop starting new work and help clear Review
wrong: Start more development to keep everyone busy
Remove the limit for this week
qa.why: The limit exists to push the team to finish work first.

qa.q: The estimate assumed the client would supply content by the 1st. It is now three weeks late. What is the best action?
qa.right: Raise it as an issue, cite the assumption and raise a change request for date and cost
wrong: Absorb the delay and compress testing
Wait to see whether the content arrives
Quietly drop the pages that need the content
qa.why: A written assumption gives a clear basis for a change request instead of an argument.

qa.q: An integration with a new provider has never been tried, and the team builds a small prototype in the first week. Which risk response is this?
qa.right: Mitigation
qa.why: A prototype reduces the likelihood of late failure without removing the integration.

qa.q: A team plans to buy insurance against a supplier failing. Which risk response is this?
qa.right: Transfer
qa.why: Transfer moves the consequence to a third party without removing the risk.

qa.q: The staging server crashed this morning and testing is blocked. How should this be logged?
qa.right: As an issue, because it has already happened
wrong: As a risk, because it might happen again
As an assumption, because the server was assumed stable
qa.why: Issues are problems that have already occurred; risks have not happened yet.

qa.q: A project was reported green for eight weeks and then missed its launch date. Which reporting pattern is the likely cause?
qa.right: Watermelon reporting
qa.why: Watermelon reporting is green on the outside and red underneath.

qa.q: Which item belongs in a team's definition of done rather than in one story's acceptance criteria?
qa.right: Code is peer reviewed and passes the automated tests
wrong: A user can reset a password using the emailed link
The report can be exported as a spreadsheet
A discount code is applied at checkout
qa.why: The definition of done applies to every item; acceptance criteria are specific to one story.

qa.q: At handover, the client's domain is registered under a developer's personal login. What should happen?
qa.right: Ownership is transferred to an account in the client's name
wrong: Nothing, because the developer can manage it for them
The developer shares the password by email
The domain is moved to the supplier's company account
qa.why: Account ownership should move to the client, not stay with an individual.

qa.q: What is the best way to give a client the credentials for their hosting?
qa.right: Through a secure channel such as a shared password manager
qa.why: Credentials move through a secure channel and never in plain text.

qa.q: On a fixed-price project the client keeps asking for small extras. What is the best protection?
qa.right: A change control process with written approval
wrong: Doing the extras to keep the relationship friendly
qa.why: Change control keeps the price tied to the agreed scope.

qa.q: In planning poker, one person shows 2 and another shows 13 for the same story. What next?
qa.right: Have the highest and lowest explain their reasoning, then vote again
wrong: Take the higher number to be safe
Let the product owner pick one
qa.why: Disagreement reveals different assumptions; discussion fixes the understanding.

qa.q: A client labels 80 percent of their requirements as Must. What is a good first step?
qa.right: Test each one by asking whether the release has any value without it
wrong: Accept the labels and plan for everything
Remove half of them at random
qa.why: A true must-have is one the release cannot do without.

qa.q: The same problem is raised in three retrospectives in a row. What is the most likely cause?
qa.right: The improvement action had no owner, date or follow-up
wrong: Retrospectives should only be held quarterly
The scrum master should assign blame
qa.why: Actions need an owner and a review at the next retrospective.

qa.q: A team does not know whether a third-party API supports bulk updates. What suits best?
qa.right: A time-boxed spike that ends with a decision or a better estimate
wrong: Estimating the story at the largest size
Starting the story and finding out later
Removing the story from the backlog
qa.why: A spike reduces uncertainty before committing.

qa.q: A team has 100 percent utilisation planned for every person. What is the likely effect?
qa.right: Any unplanned work delays everything because there is no slack
wrong: Throughput is at its maximum with no downsides
qa.why: Without headroom, queues grow sharply as soon as any extra work arrives.

qa.q: According to Moksy's customer-continuity brief, what is a challenge?
qa.right: A confirmed problem lifted off the project, versioned, with the projects joined to it
wrong: A difficult stakeholder on a project
A risk entry in the RAID log
A quote the client gave in a meeting
qa.why: A second project on the same problem is joined to the same challenge.

qa.q: What is the status of Moksy's customer-continuity design?
qa.right: It is at founder review and nothing is built yet
wrong: It is live for all customers
qa.why: The brief is a design, not live behaviour.

qa.q: A client asks Moksy for a new website. What does the continuity brief say to do before pricing?
qa.right: Play the problem back field by field in a read-back
qa.why: The ask is never the harm; it may hide a problem such as generating leads.

qa.q: Which is an item on gglearn's offboarding checklist?
qa.right: Record the answers to the ten questions only you know
qa.why: The checklist covers handover notes, ownership transfer, recorded answers and revoking access.

qa.q: In a cumulative flow diagram, the 'In test' band widens while 'Done' stays flat. What does this suggest?
qa.right: Work is piling up at testing, which is a bottleneck
wrong: The team is delivering more than before
qa.why: A widening band means more items are entering the state than leaving it.

qa.q: A team of five is planned at full utilisation and lead times keep rising. What is the most useful change?
qa.right: Reduce work in progress and leave some capacity free
wrong: Add more items to keep everyone busy
qa.why: Queues grow sharply near full load; limiting WIP shortens them.

qa.q: A team is rewarded for velocity and the points per story start to rise. Which principle explains it?
qa.right: Goodhart's law: a measure used as a target stops being a good measure
qa.why: Targeting velocity encourages inflating the points.

qa.q: A project is late and the sponsor asks to add four developers in the final month. What is the likely effect?
qa.right: The project may get later, because new people need onboarding and add communication
wrong: The project finishes four times faster
qa.why: This is Brooks's law.

qa.q: A sponsor demands a single number on day one. What is the best response?
qa.right: Give a range with its assumptions and say when it will be narrowed
wrong: Give the lowest number you can
Give the average of past projects without comment
qa.why: Early estimates must be wide, and the range shrinks as unknowns are resolved.

qa.q: Only one developer knows how to deploy. Which action reduces the bus factor risk most directly?
qa.right: Cross-train a second person and write a runbook
wrong: Ask the developer to avoid holidays
qa.why: Spreading the knowledge removes the single point of failure.

qa.q: This RAID entry has no owner. What is still missing before it can be managed?
qa.right: An owner and a planned response
qa.why: A risk is managed by a named owner with a response.
qa.code:
{
  "id": "R-14",
  "type": "risk",
  "text": "Payment provider sandbox may be unavailable during UAT",
  "probability": "medium",
  "impact": "high",
  "trigger": "Sandbox keys not issued by week 3"
}

qa.q: A sponsor asks for weekly reports of hours spent. What is a better basis for reporting?
qa.right: What was achieved against goals, with risks and decisions needed
wrong: Hours per person in more detail
qa.why: Outcome-based reporting tells stakeholders what they need to act on.

qa.q: A project is behind schedule on the critical path and the team overlaps tasks planned in sequence. What is this technique and its main downside?
qa.right: Fast tracking, which adds the risk of rework
wrong: Resource levelling, which always shortens the project
qa.why: Fast tracking overlaps tasks; crashing adds resources.

qa.q: The contractor leaves tomorrow. What is the most valuable thing to capture first?
qa.right: The knowledge that exists only in their head
wrong: The files already in the repository
A list of the meetings they attended
qa.why: Handover notes should be written while the knowledge is still in someone's head.

qa.q: Why use a Monte Carlo forecast rather than a single end date?
qa.right: It gives the probability of finishing by each date from historical throughput
wrong: It guarantees the date will be met
It removes the need for historical data
qa.why: The result is a range of dates with confidence levels.

qa.q: Budget at completion is 200 person-days, CPI is 0.8 and the trend is expected to hold. What is the estimate at completion?
qa.right: 250 person-days
qa.why: Estimate at completion is budget at completion divided by CPI: 200 / 0.8 = 250.

qa.q: A sponsor insists the plan is detailed and the team is the best, so a past-projects overrun does not apply. Which technique counters this view?
qa.right: Reference class forecasting
qa.why: It adopts an outside view based on many similar projects.

qa.q: A team says 85 percent of items finish within 8 days. An item has been in progress for 7 days. What is the best action?
qa.right: Swarm on it now, since it is about to exceed the typical cycle time
wrong: Wait, since 8 days is still normal
Add it to the next sprint
qa.why: Item age flags items at risk before they finish late.

qa.q: A mitigation for a delivery risk adds a contract with a new vendor. What can arise?
qa.right: A secondary risk created by the response itself
wrong: A residual issue that cancels the risk
A dependency that cannot be logged
A reduction in all other risks
qa.why: Responses can create new risks and dependencies.

qa.q: At kickoff a sponsor asks for a fixed end date and cost with only a one-line idea. Which concept explains why this is unsafe?
qa.right: The cone of uncertainty
qa.why: Estimates at the start are the least certain.
